subtopic: Derivatives from First Principles
context: Find the derivative of \(f\) from the first principle, where \(f\) is given by
solution:
Note that function is not defined at \(x = 2\). But, we have

\(f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\frac{2(x+h)+3}{x+h-2} - \frac{2x+3}{x-2}}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(2x+2h+3)(x-2) - (2x+3)(x+h-2)}{h(x-2)(x+h-2)}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(2x+3)(x-2) + 2h(x-2) - (2x+3)(x-2) - h(2x+3)}{h(x-2)(x+h-2)}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{-7}{(x-2)(x+h-2)} = -\frac{7}{(x-2)^2}\)

Again, note that the function \(f'\) is also not defined at \(x = 2\).

subtopic: Derivatives from First Principles
context: Find the derivative of \(f\) from the first principle, where \(f\) is given by
solution:
The function is not defined at \(x = 0\). But, we have

\(f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\left(x+h+\frac{1}{x+h}\right) - \left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left[h + \frac{1}{x+h} - \frac{1}{x}\right]\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left[h + \frac{x - x - h}{x(x+h)}\right] = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left[h\left(1 - \frac{1}{x(x+h)}\right)\right]\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\left[1 - \frac{1}{x(x+h)}\right] = 1 - \frac{1}{x^2}\)

Again, note that the function \(f'\) is not defined at \(x = 0\).

subtopic: Derivatives from First Principles
context: Find the derivative of \(f(x)\) from the first principle, where \(f(x)\) is
solution:
We have \(f'(x) = \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin(x+h) + \cos(x+h) - \sin x - \cos x}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin x \cos h + \cos x \sin h + \cos x \cos h - \sin x \sin h - \sin x - \cos x}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin h(\cos x - \sin x) + \sin x(\cos h - 1) + \cos x(\cos h - 1)}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin h}{h}(\cos x - \sin x) + \lim_{h \to 0}\sin x\frac{(\cos h - 1)}{h} + \lim_{h \to 0}\cos x\frac{(\cos h - 1)}{h}\)

\(= \cos x - \sin x\)
_note: As printed, the first line of the book's solution omits the limit sign — it reads \(f'(x) = \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\) with no \(\lim_{h \to 0}\). Transcribed faithfully; the limit reappears on the very next line.

subtopic: Derivatives from First Principles
context: Find the derivative of \(f(x)\) from the first principle, where \(f(x)\) is
solution:
\(f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(x+h)\sin(x+h) - x\sin x}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{(x+h)(\sin x \cos h + \sin h \cos x) - x \sin x}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{x\sin x(\cos h - 1) + x\cos x \sin h + h(\sin x \cos h + \sin h \cos x)}{h}\)

\(= \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{x\sin x(\cos h - 1)}{h} + \lim_{h \to 0} x\cos x\frac{\sin h}{h} + \lim_{h \to 0}(\sin x \cos h + \sin h \cos x)\)

\(= x\cos x + \sin x\)

subtopic: Algebra of Derivatives and Standard Formulas
context: Compute derivative of
solution:
Recall the trigonometric formula \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x\). Thus

\(\frac{df(x)}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(2\sin x \cos x) = 2\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x \cos x)\)

\(= 2\left[(\sin x)' \cos x + \sin x (\cos x)'\right]\)

\(= 2\left[(\cos x)\cos x + \sin x(-\sin x)\right]\)

\(= 2\left(\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x\right)\)

subtopic: Algebra of Derivatives and Standard Formulas
context: Compute derivative of
solution:
By definition, \(g(x) = \cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\). We use the quotient rule on this function wherever it is defined.

\(\frac{dg}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\right)\)

\(= \frac{(\cos x)'(\sin x) - (\cos x)(\sin x)'}{(\sin x)^2}\)

\(= \frac{(-\sin x)(\sin x) - (\cos x)(\cos x)}{(\sin x)^2}\)

\(= -\frac{\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x} = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\)

Alternatively, this may be computed by noting that \(\cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x}\). Here, we use the fact that the derivative of \(\tan x\) is \(\sec^2 x\) which we saw in Example 17 and also that the derivative of the constant function is 0.

\(\frac{dg}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{\tan x}\right)\)

\(= \frac{(1)'(\tan x) - (1)(\tan x)'}{(\tan x)^2}\)

\(= \frac{(0)(\tan x) - (\sec x)^2}{(\tan x)^2}\)

\(= \frac{-\sec^2 x}{\tan^2 x} = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\)

subtopic: Algebra of Derivatives and Standard Formulas
context: Find the derivative of
solution:
Let \(h(x) = \frac{x^5 - \cos x}{\sin x}\). We use the quotient rule on this function wherever it is defined.

\(h'(x) = \frac{(x^5 - \cos x)' \sin x - (x^5 - \cos x)(\sin x)'}{(\sin x)^2}\)

\(= \frac{(5x^4 + \sin x)\sin x - (x^5 - \cos x)\cos x}{\sin^2 x}\)

\(= \frac{-x^5 \cos x + 5x^4 \sin x + 1}{(\sin x)^2}\)

subtopic: Algebra of Derivatives and Standard Formulas
context: Find the derivative of
solution:
We use quotient rule on the function \(\frac{x + \cos x}{\tan x}\) wherever it is defined.

\(h'(x) = \frac{(x + \cos x)' \tan x - (x + \cos x)(\tan x)'}{(\tan x)^2}\)

\(= \frac{(1 - \sin x)\tan x - (x + \cos x)\sec^2 x}{(\tan x)^2}\)
